did_you_know.text: Did you know? The book of Zephaniah opens by tracing the prophet’s ancestry through four generations—Zephaniah son of Cushi, son of Gedaliah, son of Amariah, son of Hezekiah—and states that his prophecy was given during the days of Josiah king of Judah.

Did you know? At the beginning of the chapter, there is a severe declaration about gathering up and destroying everything from the face of the earth, using wording that emphasizes the sweeping scope of the judgment described.

Did you know? The description of destruction includes not only people and animals, but also the birds of the sky, the fish of the sea, and the “stumbling blocks”—everything associated with the wicked.
Did you know? The punishment in this chapter is directed specifically against Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, including the remnant of Baal worship and the priests.
Did you know? Zephaniah mentions several forms of idolatry: worshiping the host of heaven on the rooftops, and people who swear by the LORD while also swearing by their king.
Did you know? Alongside the idol worshipers, the chapter also mentions those who have turned back from following the LORD, as well as those who have not sought Him or inquired of Him.

Did you know? The day of the LORD is portrayed through the image of a sacrifice that the LORD has prepared and whose guests He has consecrated; therefore, the chapter calls out: “Hush before the Lord GOD.”

Did you know? On the day of the LORD’s sacrifice, judgment will also come upon the officials, the king’s sons, and all who wear foreign clothing—a description emphasizing that even those of high status and foreign affiliation will face judgment.
Did you know? The chapter addresses not only worship but also social injustice: it mentions those who fill their masters’ houses with violence and deceit.
Did you know? The cry of destruction is described as coming from various places in Jerusalem: from the Fish Gate, the Second Quarter, and the hills.
Did you know? The inhabitants of the Mortar are called to wail, and the chapter also connects the destruction with the disappearance of the “silver-laden”—the wealthy or the merchants.

Did you know? The LORD is portrayed as searching Jerusalem with lamps, especially examining those who say in their hearts, “The LORD will do neither good nor evil”—that is, that He does not intervene for good or for harm.

Did you know? The punishment described also affects property and life plans: the houses will become desolate, and people will build and plant vineyards, but they will not enjoy the fruits of their labor.
Did you know? The expression “The great day of the LORD is near” emphasizes the urgency of that day. It is described as coming very quickly, as a day when the bitter cry of a warrior will be heard.
Did you know? The chapter piles up many descriptions of distress: a day of wrath, trouble, devastation, darkness, gloom, clouds, and thick darkness.

Did you know? At the end of the chapter, it is stated explicitly that neither silver nor gold will be able to save anyone on the day of the LORD’s wrath; wealth offers no protection from the judgment described.
